analysis.title: The Global Week Ahead: It Won't be Lame (November 6, 2026)
key_insights: Scotiabank expects the lame duck session of Congress (before Democrats take the House and Senate after January 3rd) to be active, with possible action on USMCA/CUSMA 2.0, the December 11th funding deadline, the debt ceiling, a reconciliation bill, data centre energy costs, bank regulation, the Farm Bill and Supreme Court vacancies.

Derek Holt is cautiously optimistic on a USMCA/CUSMA 2.0 deal in the lame duck window and does not buy the narrative that Trump will double down against the agreement. PM Carney said US negotiators are 'asking less and they're offering more, but we're not quite there.' USTR Greer is reported to be pushing Trump to strike a deal with Canada.

A meaningful Canada-US trade de-escalation would lower uncertainty, lead Scotiabank to revise its growth outlook somewhat higher, reinforce its forecast of three more BoC hikes to 3.25% (possibly more), and begin to remove a discount in the undervalued C$.

Funding: a Continuing Resolution covering US$1.7 trillion of discretionary spending ends December 11th and none of the twelve appropriations bills has passed. A failure could shift control of the shutdown's shape to the new Democratic Congress. A 60-vote Senate majority is needed to avoid a filibuster, though reconciliation tied to the FY27 budget needs only a simple majority. A funding lock-in through the rest of Trump's term could reduce uncertainty but may agitate bond markets through issuance.

The federal government is about US$600 billion from the US$41.1 trillion debt ceiling. The GOP may raise or suspend it now before Democrats gain leverage. Combined with the funding deadline, it could create frictions if Trump uses it as leverage, and the administration may prefer the issue flare later under a Democratic Congress.

Democratic control raises uncertainty for bank and nonbank regulation. Private equity and private credit may face closer scrutiny, and Democrats could complicate the capital requirement changes announced in March (including the Expanded Risk-Based Approach) through oversight and hearings. There will be pressure to push easier bank regulation through before the current session ends. The Clarity Act (House response to the GENIUS Act on stablecoins) has yet to pass the Senate.

The Ratepayer Protection Act (passed the House in September, not yet the Senate) would make data centres cover the full cost of their energy demand. There may be a rush to pass it because Democrats want stronger requirements. Trump supports data centres and would presumably veto overly aggressive measures.

US CPI on Tuesday November 10 and PPI on Friday are the week's main event. They give the last inputs for the PCE estimate (release November 25) ahead of the December 9 FOMC and will set the tone for data-sensitive FOMC members. Scotiabank expects CPI +0.3% m/m SA with core similar. No official y/y rates will be published because the BLS did not publish October 2025 CPI during the shutdown. Using interpolation, total CPI y/y is roughly stable at about 3.7% and core rises to 2.9% from 2.6%.

Core services inflation is expected to stay firm, with airfare passing through energy and other costs. Goods inflation has picked up, weighted ISM price signals point to higher near-term inflation, housing inflation is expected at +0.2 to 0.3 (hotels and lodging), and vehicle prices may ease. The San Francisco Fed argues El Niño has contributed to price inflation since July, with effects fading by year-end, and markets and the Fed may struggle to see through it.

Structural drivers: the US economy is in excess demand with no output gap slack, which eases cost pass-through. Tariff pass-through continues, with ISM anecdotes citing US metals tariffs and Canadian retaliatory tariffs. AI spending lifts prices in affected categories, and shipping costs are sharply higher on Iran-war-affected routes such as Shanghai to Rotterdam.

Second-round effects may fade: nominal wage growth of about 3% y/y trails inflation, squeezing real incomes, real house prices are falling, and the saving rate is near zero in real terms. US firms respond quickly to cost pressure by cutting costs and hiring, and the US labour market has little collective bargaining, so second-round wage pressure is usually less acute than in Europe or Canada.

Central banks: only the Peru central bank (BCRP) decides this week, on Thursday. Scotiabank sees a possible 25bp hike to 4.5%, after BCRP held in October against expectations. Inflation has risen since: October headline is 5.2% and core 4.6%, both above the 1-3% target, 12-month expectations 3.1%, while core ex-transportation is at the 2% midpoint. The Central Bank Watch table lists the BCRP rate at 4.25% with Scotiabank forecasting 4.25% and the text saying a hike to 4.5% is possible.

A heavy slate of FOMC speakers (Waller, Jefferson, Goolsbee twice, Barkin, Schmid, Paulson, Hammack, Daly twice, Williams) will inform the likelihood of another hike on December 9. Normally the FOMC delivers what the September dot plot says about the year-end rate.

The Bank of Canada's Summary of Deliberations for the October 28 decision publishes Tuesday. It is expected to reinforce the hike rationale and to be stale on arrival given later GDP, jobs, oil and US midterm developments.

Global data: UK preliminary Q3 GDP on Thursday is tracking about +0.7% q/q versus 0.5% in Q2, above the BoE's expectations. The key question is whether momentum lasts into Q4 and 2027, as the OBR upgraded 2026 growth modestly and downgraded 2027 more. India's October CPI on Thursday is expected to breach the RBI's 6% upper bound, with a 25bp December hike already priced in. Mexico and Colombia CPI on Monday and Norway on Tuesday are among the last readings before their December meetings, with only Colombia expected to move.

Market backdrop: markets initially reacted favourably to the midterm results, then sentiment turned sour on AI oversight risks. Trump said he would respect the outcome and downplayed escalating the Iran war, and oil prices have since begun rising again. US Treasury markets close Wednesday for Veterans Day while the NYSE stays open, and Canadian bond markets close for Remembrance Day.

Debt ceiling standoff, with the US about US$600 billion from the limit.

Hotter-than-expected CPI or PPI would raise the chance of a December 9 Fed hike.
El Niño-driven price pressure may be treated as persistent by markets and the Fed.
Tariff pass-through, AI-related cost increases and Iran-war-driven shipping and oil costs could keep inflation elevated.
Democratic scrutiny of private equity and private credit, and of bank capital rule changes.

charts_described: Chart 1 plots US public debt against the US debt ceiling in USD trillions from 2022 to 2026, with a ceiling suspension period marked, and shows the debt approaching the US$41.1 trillion ceiling.
geopolitical: Iran war: Trump downplayed the risk of escalation after the midterms, oil prices have begun rising again, and shipping costs are higher on routes such as Shanghai to Rotterdam.
Canada-US trade: renewed USMCA/CUSMA negotiations are under way, with PM Carney saying the US is 'asking less and offering more' and USTR Greer reportedly pushing Trump to strike a deal.
US midterms: Democrats won both chambers and take control after January 3rd. Trump said he would respect the outcome.
Middle East tensions and El Niño are cited as upside inflation risks for Peru.
Possible pressure on the Supreme Court: speculation that Alito (76) and Thomas (78) could be pushed to depart in the lame duck session so Trump can fill the seats.

tension_points.theme: US inflation persistence and Fed hike
tension_points.bull_case: First-round pressures (tariffs, AI spending, shipping, excess demand with no output gap slack) are strong, core services are firm, and the Fed may hike again on December 9.
tension_points.bear_case: Second-round effects may fade: wages of about 3% lag inflation, real house prices are falling, saving is near zero, and US firms cut costs and hiring quickly. El Niño effects may dissipate by year-end.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Softer CPI on Tuesday and PPI on Friday than the 0.3% m/m expected would weaken the December hike case.

tension_points.bull_case: An active session could lock in funding through much of Trump's term, secure a USMCA 2.0 deal and settle the debt ceiling, reducing uncertainty.
tension_points.bear_case: A funding lapse after December 11th, a debt ceiling standoff and a shutdown shaped by Democrats in the new Congress.
tension_points.what_invalidates: No funding deal or continuing resolution by December 11th.
